analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum protections for people in employer health plans, including emergency care, direct specialist access, and outside appeals of denied claims.
analysis.headline: The Senate health committee approved this patients' protections bill in June 1999 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require employer health plans to cover emergency-room visits without pre-approval, let women and children see OB/GYNs and pediatricians without a referral from a gatekeeper doctor, keep patients with a doctor mid-treatment even if the plan drops that doctor, stop plans from gagging doctors, and give patients a binding appeal to outside medical experts when a claim is denied. An earlier version also gave patients the right to see and correct their own medical records and barred insurers from using genetic information against them, but those titles were scaled back or dropped as the bill moved. It applies mainly to self-insured employer plans and does not let patients sue their health plan.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of people enrolled in employer health plans, especially self-insured ones, who faced denied claims, gatekeeper referrals, and plan limits on emergency and specialist care.

how_it_helps.text: Plans must cover emergency-room screening exams without preauthorization whenever a prudent layperson would think emergency care was needed, and must cover care to stabilize the condition.
Plans that cover gynecological, obstetric, or pediatric care cannot require a referral from a primary care gatekeeper before a woman or child sees an OB/GYN or pediatrician.

A patient in the middle of treatment can keep seeing that doctor for a transition period—generally 90 days, longer for institutional care, pregnancy through postpartum, and terminal illness—even if the plan terminates the doctor's contract.
Plans cannot restrict doctors from advising patients about their health status or treatment options, even when the plan does not cover that treatment.

Plans must decide prior-authorization requests within 30 days (72 hours when time is critical), and patients who exhaust internal appeals get an external review by independent medical experts whose decision is binding on the plan.
The version introduced in January 1999 would also have let patients inspect, copy, and amend their own medical records, with civil penalties for violations.
The introduced version barred health plans from restricting enrollment or raising group premiums based on predictive genetic information about any individual.

analysis.who_pays: Health plans, insurers, and the employers who sponsor plans, through added coverage and appeals obligations that would likely be reflected in premiums.

drawbacks.text: The coverage and appeal requirements apply to plans other than 'fully insured' ones—mainly self-insured employer plans—so workers whose coverage is bought from a state-regulated insurer get little from this bill.
The bill preserves ERISA's preemption of state law, so patients still cannot sue their plan; their only remedy is administrative appeal and a limited external review.
External review is limited to denials involving medical necessity above a significant financial threshold or experimental treatment, and grievance decisions are non-appealable.
Plans may still impose cost-sharing and charge higher premiums or cost-sharing for point-of-service options, and small employers (2-50 employees) are exempt from the choice-of-coverage requirement.
The version reported by the committee dropped the medical records privacy title that was in the bill as introduced, leaving no federal access-and-correction rights in the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients in self-insured plans, the protections are real and practical—emergency coverage without pre-approval, direct access to OB/GYNs and pediatricians, continuity of care, and binding outside appeals. But the bill is deliberately limited: it carves out fully insured plans, keeps ERISA preemption so patients cannot sue, and limits external review to certain denial types, and the committee version also dropped the medical privacy title. It was the moderate Republican alternative in a debate where the central fight was whether patients could sue their plans.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate health committee approved it and put it on the Senate calendar in June 1999, but the Senate never brought it to the floor for a vote, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim Jeffords introduced the bill on January 28, 1999 with 10 Republican cosponsors, and it was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The committee held hearings on March 11, 1999, marked the bill up on March 17-18, and ordered it reported favorably.

On June 17, 1999 the committee reported the bill with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, filed written report 106-82, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 160.
The reported version dropped the personal medical information title from the bill as introduced and added formulary exceptions, specialty access, and behavioral health self-pay protections.
No vote was ever held on the bill; the action history ends with its placement on the calendar on June 17, 1999, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed-care plans, and the self-insured employers behind them, are better off because no federal patients' rights requirements were enacted from this bill.

for.name: Sen. Jim Jeffords
for.role: Senator from Vermont (R), sponsor; chairman of the Senate HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, and as committee chair led it through hearings, markup, and a favorable committee report in June 1999.

for.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings, marked up the bill, and reported it favorably to the Senate with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader and leadership in the 106th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote after it was placed on the calendar; the broader patients' bill of rights debate that summer ended without any bill passing.

against.name: Health insurance and managed-care industry
against.role: Health insurers and HMO trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed stronger patient accountability provisions, especially a right to sue health plans, during the 1999 patients' bill of rights fight.

sides.party_line_note: The bill itself was written and cosponsored entirely by Republicans (10 of 55), but the larger 1999 patients' bill of rights fight split sharply by party, with Democrats backing a bill that let patients sue their plans and Republicans backing alternatives without that right; neither became law.

industries.note: The bill would impose new coverage mandates (emergency care, direct specialist access, binding external review) on plans, but it exempts fully insured plans from most requirements and explicitly preserves ERISA preemption, so patients still could not sue—leaving the industry shielded from the accountability fights of the era.

Employers sponsoring self-insured plans would bear the compliance costs of the new coverage and appeal requirements, costs likely passed into premiums; the bill's rules are aimed directly at these plans.

industries.industry: Physicians and other health care providers
industries.note: The bill bars plans from gagging doctors on treatment advice, lets OB/GYNs and pediatricians serve patients without gatekeeper referrals, gives providers roles in formulary and appeal decisions, and protects providers from termination for letting patients self-pay for uncovered care.
